opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lucy. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, of course! Sorry if I ramble, I talk for a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI tutors are fine for practising verb endings, but you don't learn to really talk to people from an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's already hit me, to be honest. The platforms push their AI tutor first, and my rate's gone down twice this year. If it just stays here, I'll scrape by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Find more students who want proper conversation, like people moving abroad for work. Use AI to make my lesson materials faster so I can take more classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tight. Like I'm always doing sums.

S0.say: AI tutors are fine for drills, but you don't learn to really talk to people from an app.
S0.think: It has already pushed her rate down twice this year. If it stays here, she'll scrape by.
S0.do: Looks for students who want real conversation and uses AI to prep lessons faster.
S0.feel: A bit tight, always doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the platforms are using AI to squeeze tutors, and nobody's regulating them. That's the real story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow for the economy, maybe. Not slow for me. Every month the AI gets a bit better at chatting, and fewer people pay a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leave the big platforms and build my own small group of regular students. Try some in-person classes at a community centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'm good at trying new things.

S1.say: The platforms use AI to squeeze tutors, and nobody regulates them.
S1.think: It isn't slow for her. Each month the AI gets better and fewer people pay a human.
S1.do: Leaves the big platforms for her own regular students and tries in-person community classes.
S1.feel: Anxious, but good at trying new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be posting about it, honestly. Tech companies get rich, workers get crumbs, and politicians just yell. We need rules and a real safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer office workers means fewer people learning languages for work, which is a lot of my students. But maybe there are AI jobs I can do, like checking what AI tutors say in other languages. I've seen adverts for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apply for those AI language checking jobs, even if they're dull. Keep my best students. Move to a cheaper flatshare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's something to grab onto.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be helping to train the AI that's taking your work. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. It's a bit like digging my own grave and getting paid by the hour. But rent is rent.

S2.say: Tech companies get rich, workers get crumbs and politicians just yell. We need rules and a real safety net.
S2.think: Fewer office workers means fewer work-related learners, but AI language checking jobs might be something to grab.
S2.do: Applies for AI language checking jobs, keeps her best students and moves to a cheaper flatshare.
S2.feel: Worried, but with something to grab onto.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains have to be shared, through a basic income or something like it. It's not okay that some people's houses double while others lose everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI matches skilled professionals, it's definitely a good enough language teacher. The checking jobs dry up too. I'd have nothing, and I've got under a month of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look for physical work, which is still there. Bar work, maybe, or hosting tours for people visiting, where speaking languages in person still matters. Join a renters' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really scared. No safety net at all.

S3.say: The gains must be shared through a basic income or something like it.
S3.think: AI would be a good enough language teacher and the checking jobs dry up. She'd have nothing, with under a month of savings.
S3.do: Looks for bar work or in-person tour work where languages still matter, and joins a renters' group.
S3.feel: Really scared, with no safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, louder. Basic income now. It's not a fringe idea when nobody's job is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bar work, kitchens, the things I'd fall back on get robots too. What's left is being a person with people. Tours, maybe events. I'm sociable, so maybe that helps. But I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lean into anything where people pay to be with a human. Maybe move in with a friend, or back home for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, with a small hope that being human counts.

S4.say: Basic income now. It's not a fringe idea when nobody's job is safe.
S4.think: Her fallback jobs get robots too. What's left is being a person with people, and she's sociable, but she doesn't know.
S4.do: Leans into work where people pay to be with a human and considers moving in with a friend or back home.
S4.feel: Scared, with a small hope that being human counts.
